questions.question: Who were the free burghers, and why did the VOC release them in 1657?
questions.expected_answer: Former VOC employees released from their contracts and given land (about 13 ha each along the Liesbeek River) to farm as free citizens. The VOC hoped private farmers would produce more food (wheat, vegetables) more cheaply, be more motivated by profit, and help defend the station. They were limited: they had to sell to the Company at set prices, could not trade freely with ships or the Khoikhoi, had to stay 20 years and serve in the militia.

questions.question: Explain why the Huguenots came to the Cape and what contribution they made.
questions.expected_answer: French Protestants persecuted after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685; they fled to Protestant countries, and the VOC offered free passage and land at the Cape (about 200 arrived 1688-c.1700). Settled at Drakenstein and Franschhoek; contributed farming and wine-making skills; were absorbed into Dutch-speaking society (French replaced by Dutch), leaving surnames such as du Toit, du Plessis, Joubert, de Villiers.

questions.question: Why did the colonial frontier expand, and how did this affect the Khoikhoi?
questions.expected_answer: Growing burgher population and large families needed land; good land near Cape Town was taken and expensive; stock farming needed large grazing areas; loan farms (leenplase) for a fee encouraged movement inland; weak Company control far away; trade and raiding for Khoikhoi cattle. Effects: Khoikhoi lost grazing land, water and cattle; the 1713 smallpox epidemic killed many; chiefdoms near the Cape broke up and many became farm workers; the boundary moved to the Gamtoos (1770) and Great Fish River (1778).
